title: Scaling Up Thermodynamic AI Models
abstract: Thermodynamic computing devices based on the Ising model show great promise for low-power AI inference and edge computing, but scalable methods for training large models for such hardware remain limited. Prior theory shows that the time-averaged behavior of high-temperature Gibbs-sampled Ising systems can implement feed-forward neural inference. We turn this theoretical correspondence into a scalable and purely backpropagation-based algorithm for training deep convolutional networks for thermodynamic inference on Ising machine hardware. Our image classification models achieve accuracies of 94.9% on CIFAR-10 and 76.0% on CIFAR-100 under binary Gibbs sampling. We then develop and experimentally validate a mathematical theory relating inference cost to accuracy and controlling autocorrelation times. Subsequently, we calculate asymptotic results showing that inference cost is bounded by a well-controlled tradeoff with performance and exhibit algorithms for computing optimal inference schedules. Finally, we discuss implications for hardware development and the future of high-temperature thermodynamic AI models.
summary: This paper presents a novel method to train deep convolutional neural networks for inference on low-power thermodynamic hardware based on the Ising model. It achieves this by developing a scalable backpropagation algorithm that uses finite-temperature Gibbs sampling to approximate standard feed-forward computations. The work rigorously analyzes the trade-offs between computational cost (related to autocorrelation time) and classification accuracy.
main_problem: The core problem is developing scalable training methods for deep AI models intended to run on low-power, hardware-constrained thermodynamic computing devices based on the Ising model.
main_result: The authors developed a purely backpropagation-based algorithm that successfully trains deep convolutional networks, achieving high accuracy while demonstrating that inference cost can be bounded by a controllable tradeoff with performance.
method: Training involves adapting standard CNNs into blocks whose computation is approximated by finite-temperature Gibbs sampling on an Ising system, using specialized loss functions (like fixed-point losses) to stabilize the training process.
model_or_system: The model uses deep convolutional networks structured as a sequence of 'thermodynamic blocks,' where each block implements its function via stochastic dynamics (Gibbs sampling) on an Ising Hamiltonian. The system relies on mapping continuous activations to thermal mean-field averages.
key_observables: Classification accuracy (e.g., 94.9% on CIFAR-10), inference cost, and the integrated autocorrelation time ($	au_{	ext{int}}$).
important_parameters: The temperature gradient parameter $\delta$, the number of Gibbs sweeps $G$, and regularization weights ($\lambda_{FP}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the thermodynamic inference process can be accurately controlled by tuning parameters like $\delta$ and $G$ to approach the deterministic feed-forward limit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the architecture (Encoder $	o$ Thermodynamic Blocks $	o$ Decoder) for a CIFAR-10 classifier, detailing how a single block is mapped onto an Ising system with input ($s_0$), hidden ($s_1$), and output ($s_2$) spins.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical correspondence between high-temperature Gibbs sampling and feed-forward inference to developing specific training algorithms (Gibbs regularization) that stabilize this mapping, culminating in rigorous analysis of error sources like autocorrelation time.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, physics-based pathway for realizing AI hardware by embedding computation within the statistical mechanics framework of Ising models, which is highly relevant to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics and computational limits in physical systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Our CIFAR-10 classifier. The encoder is a single classical convolution with sign activation. This is followed by six thermodynamic blocks. The classical decoder is a global average pool followed by a fully- connected linear map to the output layer. Each thermodynamic block contains three convolutional layers, as depicted in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Architecture of a single thermodynamic block, implemented as an Ising system. It contains three layers of spins: input spins s0, hidden spins s1, and output spins s2. The input layer s0 is pinned in place. They are connected by bidirectional linear couplings, depicted in purple boxes. Couplings in an Ising system are bidirectional, but the labels indicate the forward coupling, i.e. moving downward in the diagram. The reverse couplings are the linear adjoint; for the exact relationship, see Equation (5). The hidden layer is also affected by the local magnetic fields b. Finally, an average-and-sign circuit a accumulates time-averages of s2 and outputs their signs.
Figure 3: Empirical |z| distribution and 3-component Gaussian mixture fit for the first block of our CIFAR- 10 model.

Figure 4: Measured stochastic error rate compared against numerically evaluated integral for the first block of our CIFAR-10 model. The fit is very close, but the integral does not capture the period-two oscillation caused by the chromatic Gibbs sampling.
Figure 5: Theoretical convergence rate for a single Gaussian spike away from z = 0, with time of transition to power-law convergence visualized.
